facts.statement: The genus Nicrosaurus was described by the German paleontologist Oscar Fraas in 1866.
facts.quote: authority: Fraas, 1866

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus lived during the Late Triassic period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Triassic,

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus is an extinct genus of phytosaur reptile.
facts.quote: Nicrosaurus (/nɪkroʊˈsɔrəs/) is an extinct genus of phytosaur reptile

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus resembled crocodiles but was not closely related to them, representing an example of parallel evolution.
facts.quote: Although it looked like a crocodile (and probably lived like the more terrestrial crocodylomorphs), it was not closely related to them, instead being an example of parallel evolution.

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus nostrils were positioned directly in front of the forehead, similar to modern cetaceans, unlike crocodiles where they are at the snout tip.
facts.quote: Nicrosauruss nostrils, or external nares, were placed directly in front of the forehead (much like modern-day cetaceans, such as whales, dolphins, and porpoises), whereas in crocodiles, the nostrils are positioned on the end of the snout.

facts.statement: The name Nicrosaurus was possibly derived from the Neckar river in southwestern Germany where fossils were found.
facts.quote: The genus was named by German paleontologist, Oscar Fraas, in 1866, possibly after the Neckar river of southwestern Germany, near which it was found.

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus possessed external nares at the skull roof level, a broad heavy rostrum, and a strong prenarial crest.
facts.quote: Some distinguishing anatomical features of Nicrosaurus are the external nares at the skull roof level, the dorsoventrally compressed and rounded posterior squamosal processes, the broad and heavy rostrum and a strong prenarial crest.

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus was likely a secondarily terrestrial predator with a deep upper jaw and heterodont teeth, similar to terrestrial crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: Combined with its unusually deep upper jaw and heterodont teeth, it was most likely a secondarily terrestrial predator, probably not at all dissimilar from terrestrial crocodylomorphs like sebecians.

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus had highly heterodont dentition ranging from wide blade teeth to cylindrical recurved caniniform teeth.
facts.quote: Nicrosaurus dentition is highly heterodont, the tooth shapes varying from wide, laterally compressed blade teeth to cylindrical, recurved caniniform teeth.

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus had massive snouts similar to modern crocodilians, suggesting it preyed on tetrapods rather than fish.
facts.quote: Nicrosaurus in general have massive snouts similar to extant crocodilians, suggesting they preyed on tetrapods instead of fish.

facts.statement: The proximal end of the humerus in Nicrosaurus is flattened.
facts.quote: In Nicrosaurus, the proximal end the humerus is flattened.

facts.statement: Recent analysis of post-cranial bones supports the idea that Nicrosaurus was primarily terrestrial.
facts.quote: A more recent analysis on available post-cranial bones has provided results that further support the idea of Nicrosaurus being primarily terrestrial.

facts.statement: The ilium and femur of Nicrosaurus resemble terrestrial archosaurs, suggesting it had an upright walking style.
facts.quote: The ilium and femur of Nicrosaurus are similar to those of Archosaurs in comparison to semi-aquatic Archosaurs, like today's crocodiles. The resemblance suggests Nicrosaurus could have had a more upright walking style that is often associated with terrestrial organisms.

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus fossils were found in arkosic sandstones and lacustrine sandstones, indicating a freshwater river habitat.
facts.quote: Nicrosaurus and Mystriosuchus have both been recovered in the first and second Stubensandstein in arkosic sandstones separated by floodplain mudstones and were both buried during flooding events in a freshwater river habitat.

facts.statement: It was initially debated that phytosaurs were semi-aquatic with a fish-based diet due to their resemblance to modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: Because of their resemblance to modern crocodiles, it was initially thought that phytosaurs were also semi-aquatic animals. The slender jaws further suggested a diet containing fish.

facts.statement: A 2013 study found that the ilium of Nicrosaurus is distinctive from all other phytosaurs.
facts.quote: A 2013 study has also found that the ilium of Nicrosaurus is quite distinctive from all other phytosaurs.

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus tooth rows usually consist of 40 to 45 teeth.
facts.quote: Teeth rows usually consist of 40-45 members.

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus kapffi likely had a mixed diet that included both fish and tetrapods based on microwear patterns on its teeth.
facts.quote: A study on phytosaur microwear patterns shows that both Nicrosaurus species had mixed diets, with Nicrosaurus kapffi probably consuming both fish and tetrapods

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus meyeri had dietary habits similar to N. kapffi, overlapping with carnivores, fish-eaters, and consumers of hard-shelled invertebrates.
facts.quote: Nicrosaurus meyeri generally plotting in similar areas of the texture–dietary spaces as N. kapffi, overlapping most strongly with carnivores, piscivores, and hard invertebrate consumers

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus kapffi and N. meyeri fossils are found in the Norian-aged Stubensandstein of southwestern Germany and the Norian Arnstadt Formation.
facts.quote: Species Nicrosaurus kapffi and the less commonly found Nicrosaurus meyeri occur in the Norian Stubensandstein of southwestern Germany, as well as from the Norian Arnstadt Formation

facts.statement: The Arnstadt Formation where Nicrosaurus fossils are found is a lake-based sedimentary sequence in the Germanic Basin.
facts.quote: The Arnstadt Formation, or "Steinmergelkeuper", is primarily a lacustrine sedimentary succession of the Germanic Basin

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus fossils from Germany were discovered in environments associated with rivers, lakes, or dry floodplains.
facts.quote: Fossil discoveries in Germany were found in dry floodplain environments or fluvial lacustrine indet., where the environment was known to be associated with either rivers or lakes or both

facts.statement: An isolated Nicrosaurus tooth found in 2002 among fish scales suggests the animal may have lived in swampy areas or scavenged dead fish.
facts.quote: An isolated tooth found in a bed among fish scales in the middle part of Arnstadt Formation in 2002 was attributed to Nicrosaurus

facts.statement: A 2002 study placed the genera Machaeroprosopus, Mystriosuchus, Redondasaurus, and Nicrosaurus within the clade Mystriosuchini.
facts.quote: A 2002 phylogenetic analysis found that the genera Machaeroprosopus, Mystriosuchus, Redondasaurus and Nicrosaurus are all under the clade Mystriosuchini

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus is considered the most basal (earliest branching) member of the Mystriosuchini clade.
facts.quote: Nicrosaurus is considered the most basal taxon of the clade

facts.statement: The genus Nicrosaurus was named by Fraas in 1866.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Nicrosaurus (genus), Fraas 1866

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus belongs to the parent group Mystriosuchini.
facts.quote: Parent group: Mystriosuchini

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus is classified within the family Parasuchidae.
facts.quote: Family: Parasuchidae

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus is classified as a reptile.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus lived during the Norian to Rhaetian stages, from 227.3 to 201.4 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Norian to Rhaetian (227.3 to 201.4 million years ago)

facts.statement: Herbert E. Gregory originally assigned the species Rutiodon gregorii to the genus Nicrosaurus.
facts.quote: Herbert E. Gregory referred Rutiodon gregorii to Nicrosaurus

facts.statement: The species previously known as Phytosaurus gregorii was later reclassified as Nicrosaurus gregorii due to skull similarities.
facts.quote: Phytosaurus gregorii was later assigned as Nicrosaurus gregorii because of observed similarities in skull characteristics

facts.statement: Some skulls found in the Chinle Formation were incorrectly identified as Nicrosaurus rather than the genus Rutiodon.
facts.quote: Some of the skulls discovered in this region were said to be incorrectly assigned to Nicrosaurus instead of Rutiodon

facts.statement: The first North American phytosaur taxon, originally named Belodon buceros in 1881, was found in the Chama basin of New Mexico.
facts.quote: The first phytosaur taxon discovered in North America was believed to be from a skull of Belodon buceros in 1881 in the Chama basin, of north-central New Mexico

facts.statement: The species B. buceros has been attributed to various genera including Pseudopalatus, Phytosaurus, Machaeroprosopus, Arribasuchus, and Nicrosaurus.
facts.quote: The species has also been attributed to other genera, including Pseudopalatus, Phytosaurus, Machaeroprosopus, Arribasuchus and Nicrosaurus

facts.statement: Some scientists attributed the skull of B. buceros to Nicrosaurus based on characteristics of the squamosal bone and supra-temporal fenestra.
facts.quote: Some attributed the skull type to Nicrosaurus because of a few cranial characteristics, pertaining to the squamosal and supra-temporal fenestra

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus buceros was distinguished from N. kapffi by having a narrower snout.
facts.quote: In comparison to Nicrosaurus kapffi, it carried a more narrow snout and therefore was referred to as Nicrosaurus buceros by some scientists

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus kapffi was originally described by Meyer in 1860.
facts.quote: Nicrosaurus kapffi (Meyer, 1860): SMNS 4378, 4379, 5726, 5727; NHMUK PV OR 43743

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus meyeri was described by Hungerbühler and Hunt in 2000.
facts.quote: Nicrosaurus meyeri (Hungerbühler and Hunt, 2000): SMNS 12598 (holotype), 4059; NHMUK PV OR 42745

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus kapffi is characterized by a long snout, a ventrally convex alveolar rim of the maxilla, and a tripartite upper dentition.
facts.quote: Nicrosaurus kapffi Long snout Ventrally convex alveolar rim of maxilla Tripartite upper dentition

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus meyeri is characterized by a very long snout and a bipartite upper dentition.
facts.quote: Nicrosaurus meyeri Very long snout Bipartite upper dentition

facts.statement: Nicrosaurus specimens have been found in various rock types including sandstone, marl, dolomite, breccia, and claystone.
facts.quote: Specimen have been found in various bed lithology, including sandstone, marl, dolomite, breccia, and claystone

facts.statement: Scientific literature mentions two additional species, Nicrosaurus gregorii and Nicrosaurus buceros, beyond the two primary species.
facts.quote: Beyond the Nicrosaurus kapffi and Nicrosaurus meyeri, there are two other species mentioned in scientific literature: Nicrosaurus gregorii and Nicrosaurus buceros

facts.statement: The remains of Nicrosaurus gregorii and Nicrosaurus buceros were found in the Chama basin of north-central New Mexico.
facts.quote: The remains of the latter two were found in North America, from the Chama basin of north-central New Mexico

rejected.quote: Nicrosaurus may have been more terrestrial than other phytosaurs. Occurring in marginal-lacustrine or outrightly terrestrial settings, it bears longer limb bones, a straighter femur and a deeper pelvis than other phytosaurs.
